QUICK · 15 s
SAY:
• Good morning. We are Chaitanya Shinde, Amit Ingle, Sumant Vetal and Sahil Chavan, guided by Prof. V. D. Dhore.
• Our project: AgriAgent, a safety-gated zero-shot vision pipeline for crop–weed spot spraying.
BOOK: title page
2:
EXPLAIN · 45 s
SAY:
• Farmers spray herbicide on the whole field, although weeds grow in patches.
• A spot sprayer opens a nozzle only above a weed. The nozzle is cheap; the decision weed-or-crop is the bottleneck.
• Two errors are not equal: a missed weed survives one pass; a crop plant called 'weed' gets sprayed.
• So our main number is how much crop lands on the spray map.
IF ASKED: Why is crop damage worse? A missed weed is caught next pass; a sprayed crop plant is lost yield.
BOOK: §1.1, p. 1
3:
EXPLAIN · 45 s
SAY:
• Trained networks do this well, but need labelled photos from the same field and drop on new fields.
• Zero-shot models promise no labels: Grounding DINO finds objects named in text, SAM 2 outlines them. Together: Grounded SAM.
• Then read the problem statement box.
IF ASKED: Zero-shot = pretrained by others on huge general data, no training on our photos. We trained nothing.
BOOK: §1.2–1.3, pp. 1–2

EXPLAIN · 40 s

• Ren et al. 2024, Grounded SAM: the pipeline we implement.
• VLM studies: 0.15–0.75 accuracy, so VLMs may advise, not decide.
BOOK: Ch. 2, pp. 3–17; Table 2.1, p. 16

SAY:
• Base paper: Grounded SAM. We implement it, with SAM 2 instead of SAM.

BOOK: §3.1, p. 19
10:
EXPLAIN · 30 s
SAY:
• Six objectives, three research questions.
• RQ1: how well does Grounded SAM separate weed from crop?
• RQ2: does asking AI models about unsure plants help without making it less safe?
• RQ3: which cheap addition cuts crop damage most, at what cost?
• The rest of the talk answers these three.
CLOCK: be here by 5:00.
BOOK: Ch. 4, pp. 20–21
11:
EXPLAIN · 50 s
SAY (point at the diagram, top to bottom):
• Photo + crop name → Grounding DINO boxes → SAM 2 masks → plant rules → safety gate (yellow) → app and GeoJSON.
• System 1 runs on the laptop, 0.6 s per photo, same input same output.
• System 2 (blue, cloud) only advises.
• The yellow gate is the only part allowed to approve spraying.
IF ASKED: Why two systems? Local plain code decides; cloud AI can be wrong, so it may only advise.
BOOK: §5.2, p. 23, Fig. 5.1
12:
EXPLAIN · 40 s
SAY:
• The gate is plain code, not AI.
• Sprays a mask only if: label says weed and not the crop; confidence ≥ 0.70; mask quality ≥ 0.85; covers ≤ 50% of the photo.
• If more than 85% would be sprayed, nothing is. Any error → do not spray.
• An early version passed confidence as 1.0 and sprayed every 'weed'; we found and fixed it, and now every rule has a test with real values.
IF ASKED: Why not AI here? Spraying the crop is the costly mistake; rules are testable, explainable, repeatable.
BOOK: §5.3, p. 23; equations §6.1.6, p. 30
13:
EXPLAIN · 45 s
SAY:
• The detector rarely boxes small weeds, so we check every green patch (excess green + Otsu threshold).
• Rule 1: crop if ≥ 30% inside a crop mask. Rule 2: crop if on the planting row.
• Rule 3: weed if smaller than ¼ of the median crop plant. Rule 4: weed if no crop was found and it is off the row.
• Anything else: unsure, never sprayed.
• Written on 30 photos, frozen, then run once on 90 new photos.
IF ASKED: Why ¼? It calibrates itself per photo; set by design, never tuned on held-out photos.
BOOK: §5.4, p. 24
14:
QUICK · 30 s
SAY:
• Escalation agent: asks up to three sources (row rule, Clef Flash, Qwen) about withheld plants, cheapest first; needs 85% for 'weed'; only advises.
• System 2 names the weed, but the herbicide and dose come only from the ICAR–DWR bulletin; banned herbicides rejected.
• Farmer summary in English, Hindi, Marathi.
IF ASKED: Is it an agent? One bounded agent: picks which source to ask next under a call budget, keeps a trace, has no authority.
BOOK: §5.5–5.7, pp. 24–25

17:
EXPLAIN · 75 s (live demo, or this slide as the backup)
SAY (walk the five panels left to right):
• ① A real development photo, crop = sugar beet.
• ② Grounding DINO draws one box over the whole photo, 'sugar beet plant' 0.58: its labels are useless here.
• ③ SAM 2 turns it into one mask, the whole photo.

18:
QUICK · 30 s
SAY:
• The full model is in §6.1.
• Excess green = 2G − R − B; Otsu picks the plant/soil threshold per photo; rows come from the vegetation profile.
• The classifier is a piecewise function; line 5 applies only when no crop was found: our known failure F1.
IF ASKED: Otsu? Tries every threshold and keeps the one that best separates the two pixel groups (max between-class variance).
BOOK: §6.1.2–6.1.5, pp. 29–30
19:
QUICK · 30 s
SAY:
• The gate is an AND of conditions.
• The agent multiplies odds: Clef (0.70) and Qwen (0.80) both say weed → odds 9.33 → P = 0.90 ≥ 0.85 → weed. One source alone tops out at 0.80.
• Metrics are pixel ratios, tested on a 5×5 toy grid: crop 2/6 = 33.3%, recall 3/4 = 75%, saved 80%.
IF ASKED: Weights 0.80/0.70/0.65 = measured accuracies 16/20, 14/20, 13/20.
BOOK: §6.1.6–6.1.8, pp. 30–31

SAY:

• The deployed 0.70 sprays nothing, because real scores never pass 0.68.

22:
EXPLAIN · 45 s
SAY:
• On 90 photos never used in design: 77.9% weed recall at 8.8% crop sprayed, against 1.8% and 65.5% for Grounded SAM.
• 95% herbicide saved.
• 95% intervals for weeds hit: 76.7–86.8% vs 0.5–4.0%, no overlap.

IF ASKED: Why is 77.9 outside 76.7–86.8? The interval counts weeds hit (177/215 = 82.3%); 77.9% counts weed pixels.
